subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to the visual world of mathematics! In this unit you will learn how graphs turn numbers and relationships into pictures. A graph can show at a glance something that a long list of numbers hides. When Amina plots the temperature in Hargeisa hour by hour, when Yusuf tracks how far a bus has travelled from Mogadishu over time, or when Halima works out the cost of buying mangoes at the Eastleigh market, they are all using the ideas in this unit.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Lower Secondary Mathematics 0862 — Stage 7 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Plot and read points in all four quadrants using ordered pairs (x, y).
Name the axes, the origin, and the four quadrants correctly.
Understand a linear function and the meaning of y = mx + c.
Calculate a gradient (slope) as a rate of change and find a y-intercept.
Draw a straight-line graph using a table of values and using gradient and intercept.
Read values from a graph, including interpolation and extrapolation.
Find the point where two lines intersect and explain what it means.
Interpret real-life graphs such as distance–time and cost graphs.
Recognise and draw straight-line graphs that are parallel to an axis, such as x = 3 (a vertical line) and y = −2 (a horizontal line).

concepts.title: The Coordinate Plane
concepts.explanation: The grid we use for graphing is called the coordinate plane, or the Cartesian plane after the French mathematician René Descartes. It is built from two number lines that cross at right angles. The horizontal line is the x-axis; positive numbers run to the right and negative numbers to the left. The vertical line is the y-axis; positive numbers run upward and negative numbers downward. The point where they cross is the origin, written (0, 0). To plot the point (3, 2), start at the origin, move 3 units right along the x-axis, then 2 units up, and mark the point.

concepts.title: Functions and Relationships
concepts.explanation:
A function is a rule that links two quantities so that each input gives exactly one output. Think of a function as a machine: you put a number in, the machine follows its rule, and one number comes out. If the rule is “multiply by 2, then add 1”, then putting in 3 gives 2×3 + 1 = 7. We can write this rule as an equation, y = 2x + 1, where x is the input and y is the output.

The input is called the independent variable because you are free to choose it, and the output is called the dependent variable because its value depends on your choice. In a journey, time is usually the independent variable (you decide which moment to look at) and distance is the dependent variable (it depends on how long you have travelled). We normally put the independent variable on the horizontal x-axis and the dependent variable on the vertical y-axis.

One relationship can be shown in several matching ways, and a strong mathematician can move between them:

In words: “y is one more than twice x.”

As a table of values: pairs of x and y that fit the rule.

As a graph: a line or curve on the coordinate plane.
concepts.example: A table of values is the bridge between an equation and a graph. To build one, choose some x-values, put each into the rule, and record the y-value it produces. For y = 2x + 1: when x = 0, y = 1; when x = 1, y = 3; when x = 2, y = 5. This gives the points (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 5), which we can then plot. Each point is a single example of the rule; the full graph shows *every* example at once. That is the quiet power of a graph – it holds an endless list of number pairs in one picture.

concepts.title: Linear Functions and y = mx + c
concepts.explanation:
A linear function is one whose graph is a perfectly straight line. Every linear function can be written in the form y = mx + c, where m is the gradient (how steep the line is) and c is the y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis). These two numbers tell you everything you need to draw the line, so it is worth understanding each one carefully.

The sign of the gradient tells you the direction of the line:

Positive gradient (m > 0): the line goes up from left to right.

Negative gradient (m < 0): the line goes down from left to right.

Zero gradient (m = 0): the line is horizontal, like y = 3.

A vertical line such as x = 2 has an undefined gradient, because x never changes.

The y-intercept c is the value of y when x = 0, so it is where the line meets the y-axis. In y = 3x + 5, putting x = 0 gives y = 5, so the line crosses the y-axis at the point (0, 5). In a real situation the y-intercept is often a starting amount: a fixed charge before any distance is travelled, or the water already in a tank before it begins to fill.
concepts.example: Let us read a full equation. In y = 2x − 1, the gradient is 2 and the y-intercept is −1. So the line crosses the y-axis at (0, −1) and, from there, climbs 2 units for every 1 unit across. Compare this with y = −0.5x + 4, whose gradient is −0.5 (a gentle downward slope) and whose y-intercept is 4. Just by reading m and c you can already picture each line before drawing a single point. Two lines with the same gradient are parallel – they never meet – which is why y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 run side by side forever.

concepts.title: Drawing Straight-Line Graphs
concepts.explanation: There are two reliable methods for drawing the graph of a linear function. Learn both, because each is quicker in different situations. Choose three or four x-values, work out each matching y-value, plot the points, and join them with a ruled straight line. Three points is enough, and the third acts as a check: if the three do not lie in a straight line, one of them is wrong. For y = 2x − 1 we might choose x = 0, 1, 2 and 3, giving y = −1, 1, 3 and 5. That produces the points (0, −1), (1, 1), (2, 3) and (3, 5).… Two special straight lines do not fit the table-of-values pattern above, because they only involve one variable. The equation x = 3 means 'the x-coordinate is always 3, whatever y is' — this draws a vertical line passing through 3 on the x-axis, parallel to the y-axis. The equation y = −2 means 'the y-coordinate is always −2, whatever x is' — this draws a horizontal line passing through −2 on the y-axis, parallel to the x-axis. These lines are easy to spot: if the equation only contains x, the line is vertical; if it only contains y, the line is horizontal.
concepts.example: Always label your axes with the variable and any units, choose a sensible scale so the line fills the grid, and extend the line a little beyond your points with arrows to show it continues. A graph without labels is… To draw y = 4, rule a horizontal line through every point where the y-coordinate is 4, such as (−2, 4), (0, 4) and (3, 4). To draw x = −1, rule a vertical line through every point where the x-coordinate is −1, such as (−1, −3), (−1, 0) and (−1, 5).

concepts.title: Reading and Interpreting Graphs
concepts.explanation:
Drawing a graph is only half the skill; the other half is reading one that is already drawn. Graphs answer questions quickly once you know how to look.

Direct reading finds a value straight from the line. To answer “what is y when x = 4?”, go up from 4 on the x-axis until you meet the line, then across to the y-axis to read the value. To answer “when is y = 10?”, do the reverse: start at 10 on the y-axis, go across to the line, then down to the x-axis.

Interpolation means reading a value between points you already know – for example estimating the temperature at 2:30 pm when you have readings at 2:00 and 3:00. Because the values sit inside the data, interpolation is usually trustworthy. Extrapolation means extending the line beyond the data to predict a value – for example guessing the temperature at 6:00 pm from readings that stop at 4:00. Extrapolation can be useful but is riskier, because the pattern may not continue; a plant that grows steadily for a week will not keep growing at the same rate forever.

The gradient of a real graph carries meaning. On a distance–time graph the gradient is the speed; a steeper line means faster travel, and a horizontal segment means the object is not moving at all. On a cost graph the gradient is the price per unit. Always ask what the steepness of a line is telling you about the situation, not just about the numbers.
concepts.example: Two lines drawn on the same axes may cross. The point of intersection is the one pair (x, y) that fits both rules at the same time. If Omar's savings follow one line and his brother Idris's follow another, the point where the lines cross is the moment their savings are equal. We can check an intersection with algebra: to find where y = 2x + 1 meets y = −x + 4, set 2x + 1 = −x + 4, giving 3x = 3, so x = 1 and y = 3. The lines meet at (1, 3), exactly where the graph shows.

concepts.title: Real-Life Graphs
concepts.explanation:
The reason graphs matter is that they describe the real world. Many everyday situations follow a linear rule, and putting them on a graph makes the story easy to read.

Distance–time graphs show a journey. Time goes on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis. A straight sloping line means steady speed; the steeper the line, the faster the travel. A flat, horizontal line means a stop – time passes but distance does not change. Suppose Hassan cycles from his home towards the masjid at a steady 12 km/h. After t hours he has travelled d = 12t kilometres, a straight line through the origin with gradient 12. If he rests for a while, the graph is flat during the rest, then slopes up again when he sets off.

Cost graphs often have a fixed charge plus a rate. A taxi in Nairobi might charge a flat 200 shillings plus 100 shillings per kilometre. The cost of a journey of d kilometres is C = 100d + 200. Here the y-intercept 200 is the fixed charge you pay before moving at all, and the gradient 100 is the price of each extra kilometre. Reading the graph, you can find the cost of any journey, or work backwards from a budget to see how far you can afford to travel.

Conversion graphs turn one unit into another. Because the rule is linear, a single straight line lets you convert either way just by reading across and up. For example, converting temperatures with F = 1.8C + 32 gives a straight line: the gradient 1.8 shows that each 1°C rise is a 1.8°F rise, and the y-intercept 32 shows that 0°C equals 32°F. The same idea converts between shillings and dollars, or kilometres and miles: draw the line once, then read off any conversion you need.

You have now met six connected ideas: the coordinate plane, functions and tables, the form y = mx + c, drawing straight lines, reading graphs, and real-life graphs. These are not separate topics – they are one story told in different ways. An equation such as C = 100d + 200 becomes a table of values, the table becomes plotted points, the points become a line, and the line lets you read off answers to real questions about a taxi fare. Being able to travel in any direction round this circle – from equation to graph and back again – is what it means to truly understand graphs.
concepts.example: The best way to fix these ideas in your memory is to use them with real numbers around you. Time a walk to the shop and sketch the distance–time graph. Work out the cost of buying different numbers of mangoes and plot the line. Every time you connect a graph to something real, your understanding grows stronger, and the harder mathematics of later years – simultaneous equations, quadratic curves, and eventually calculus – will feel like familiar ground. Now let us practise together with some worked examples.

methods.title: How to draw a line from y = mx + c
methods.example: In which quadrant does the point (−3, 5) lie?
steps: Plot the y-intercept c on the y-axis.
From there, use the gradient m: go 1 right and m up (or down if m is negative).
Mark a second and third point the same way.
Rule a straight line through the points and label it.

methods.title: How to find where a line crosses each axis
methods.example: Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11).
steps: For the y-intercept, set x = 0 and work out y.
For the x-intercept, set y = 0 and solve for x.
Plot both points and rule the line through them.

methods.title: How to find where two lines meet
methods.example: State the gradient and y-intercept of y = −2x + 7.
steps: Set the two right-hand sides equal to each other.
Solve the equation to find x.
Put x back into either equation to find y.
Write the intersection as the point (x, y) and check it in the other equation.

methods.title: Build a table of values
methods.example: Complete a table for y = 3x − 1 using x = −1, 0, 1, 2.
steps: When x = 0, y = −1.
When x = 1, y = 2.
When x = 2, y = 5.

methods.title: Find an x-intercept
methods.example: Where does the line y = 2x − 6 cross the x-axis?
steps: On the x-axis, y = 0.
So 0 = 2x − 6, giving 2x = 6 and x = 3.
The line crosses the x-axis at the point (3, 0).

methods.title: Find where two lines meet
methods.example: Find the intersection of y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7.
steps: At the crossing point both y-values are equal, so 2x + 1 = −x + 7.
Add x to both sides: 3x + 1 = 7.
Subtract 1: 3x = 6, so x = 2.

workedExamples.title: Name the quadrant
workedExamples.prompt: In which quadrant does the point (−3, 5) lie?
workedExamples.solution: The x-coordinate −3 is negative (left) and the y-coordinate 5 is positive (up). Left and up is the top-left region, which is Quadrant II.

workedExamples.title: Calculate a gradient
workedExamples.prompt: Find the gradient of the line through (2, 3) and (6, 11).
workedExamples.solution: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x = (11 − 3) ÷ (6 − 2) = 8 ÷ 4 = 2. The line rises 2 units for every 1 unit across.

workedExamples.title: Read m and c
workedExamples.prompt: State the gradient and y-intercept of y = −2x + 7.
workedExamples.solution: The number in front of x is the gradient, so m = −2 (a downward slope). The constant term is the y-intercept, so c = 7, meaning the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 7).

workedExamples.title: Build a table of values
workedExamples.prompt: Complete a table for y = 3x − 1 using x = −1, 0, 1, 2.
workedExamples.solution: When x = −1, y = 3(−1) − 1 = −4. When x = 0, y = −1. When x = 1, y = 2. When x = 2, y = 5. The points are (−1, −4), (0, −1), (1, 2) and (2, 5). Plotted, they lie in a straight line.

workedExamples.title: Find an x-intercept
workedExamples.prompt: Where does the line y = 2x − 6 cross the x-axis?
workedExamples.solution: On the x-axis, y = 0. So 0 = 2x − 6, giving 2x = 6 and x = 3. The line crosses the x-axis at the point (3, 0).

workedExamples.title: Find where two lines meet
workedExamples.prompt: Find the intersection of y = 2x + 1 and y = −x + 7.
workedExamples.solution: At the crossing point both y-values are equal, so 2x + 1 = −x + 7. Add x to both sides: 3x + 1 = 7. Subtract 1: 3x = 6, so x = 2. Then y = 2(2) + 1 = 5. The lines meet at (2, 5). Check: −x + 7 = −2 + 7 = 5. ✓

workedExamples.title: Interpret a real-life graph
workedExamples.prompt: A taxi fare is C = 100d + 200 (shillings, for d kilometres). Find the fare for 6 km, and explain the numbers 100 and 200.
workedExamples.solution: C = 100(6) + 200 = 600 + 200 = 800 shillings. The 200 is the fixed charge before the taxi moves (the y-intercept). The 100 is the cost of each kilometre (the gradient).

workedExamples.title: Read a distance–time graph
workedExamples.prompt: On a distance–time graph, a line rises steadily from (0, 0) to (2, 24), where distance is in km and time in hours. What is the speed?
workedExamples.solution: Speed is the gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time = 24 ÷ 2 = 12 km/h. The line is straight, so the speed is constant throughout.

workedExamples.title: Write an equation from gradient and intercept
workedExamples.prompt: Write the equation of the line with gradient 3 that crosses the y-axis at (0, −2).
workedExamples.solution: Using y = mx + c with m = 3 and y-intercept c = −2, the equation is y = 3x − 2.

workedExamples.title: State whether each pair of lines is parallel
workedExamples.prompt: State whether each pair of lines is parallel: a) y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 5 b) y = 3x and y = −3x.
workedExamples.solution: a) Both lines have gradient 2, so they are parallel. b) The gradients are 3 and −3, which are different, so these lines are not parallel.

workedExamples.title: Interpret a distance-time graph
workedExamples.prompt: On a distance–time graph, describe what each part means: a) a steep upward line b) a flat horizontal line.
workedExamples.solution: a) A steep upward line means the object is moving away quickly — a fast, steady speed (a large positive gradient). b) A flat horizontal line means the object has stopped; time is passing but the distance is not changing.

workedExamples.title: Check an intersection by substitution
workedExamples.prompt: Find where y = 3x − 1 and y = x + 5 intersect, and check your answer by substitution.
workedExamples.solution: 3x − 1 = x + 5 → 2x = 6 → x = 3. Then y = 3(3) − 1 = 8. The lines meet at (3, 8). Check: x + 5 = 3 + 5 = 8 ✓.

activities.title: Make a Giant Coordinate Grid
activities.materials: a large sheet of paper or chalk on the ground, a ruler, and small stones as markers.
steps: Draw two number lines crossing at right angles to make x- and y-axes, numbered from −5 to 5.
Call out coordinates like (3, −2) and place a stone at each point.
Ask a partner (or your AI tutor, or check it yourself) to name the quadrant of every stone you place.
Join four stones to make a square or rectangle, then read off all four corner coordinates.
Keep your grid – you can use it for the plotting games below.

activities.title: Coordinate Picture Puzzle
steps: Choose a simple shape – a house, a boat, or a star.
Draw it on the grid and write down the coordinates of each corner in order.
Give only the list of coordinates to a friend or your AI tutor, and let them plot and join the points.
Compare their picture with your original. Did the coordinates describe it exactly?

activities.title: The Gradient Walk
activities.materials: an outdoor space and a way to measure steps.
steps: Walk at a steady pace and have a partner, or a phone timer with beeps, call out the time every 10 seconds.
Count how many steps you have taken at each call and record the pairs (time, steps).
Plot the points on squared paper – they should lie roughly on a straight line.
Work out the gradient (steps per second). That gradient is your walking speed!
Try walking faster and slower and see how the steepness of the line changes.

activities.title: Taxi Fare Investigation
activities.materials: paper, pencil, and a made-up fare rule.
steps: Invent a taxi rule, for example a 200-shilling fixed charge plus 100 shillings per kilometre.
Make a table of the fare for 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 kilometres.
Plot the points and rule a straight line through them.

rules.title: Defining a Function
rules.text: A function is a rule that links two quantities so that each input gives exactly one output. Think of a function as a machine: you put a number in, the machine follows its rule, and one number comes out. If the rule is “multiply by 2, then add 1”, then putting in 3 gives 2×3 + 1 = 7. We can write this rule as an equation, y = 2x + 1, where x is the input and y is the output.

rules.title: Building a Table of Values
rules.text: A table of values is the bridge between an equation and a graph. To build one, choose some x-values, put each into the rule, and record the y-value it produces. For y = 2x + 1: when x = 0, y = 1; when x = 1, y = 3; when x = 2, y = 5. This gives the points (0, 1), (1, 3) and (2, 5), which we can then plot. Each point is a single example of the rule; the full graph shows *every* example at once. That is the quiet power of a graph – it holds an endless list of number pairs in one picture.

rules.title: Plotting from a Table of Values
rules.text: Choose three or four x-values, work out each matching y-value, plot the points, and join them with a ruled straight line. Three points is enough, and the third acts as a check: if the three do not lie in a straight line, one of them is wrong. For y = 2x − 1 we might choose x = 0, 1, 2 and 3, giving y = −1, 1, 3 and 5. That produces the points (0, −1), (1, 1), (2, 3) and (3, 5). Plot them and rule a line through all four.

rules.title: Reading m and c from an Equation
rules.text: Read m and c straight from the equation. Plot the y-intercept first, then use the gradient to step to more points. For y = 2x − 1: plot the intercept at (0, −1). The gradient is 2 = 2/1, so from (0, −1) move 1 right and 2 up to reach (1, 1); repeat to reach (2, 3). Rule the line. For a negative gradient such as −3, you step 1 right and 3 down each time.

rules.title: Using the Two Intercepts
rules.text: A third handy idea is to use the two intercepts. Find the y-intercept by setting x = 0, and the x-intercept by setting y = 0, then rule a line through both. For y = 2x − 6, setting x = 0 gives (0, −6) and setting y = 0 gives 0 = 2x − 6, so x = 3 and the point (3, 0). Two well-separated points are all you need for a straight line.

rules.title: Why Real-Life Graphs Matter
rules.text: The reason graphs matter is that they describe the real world. Many everyday situations follow a linear rule, and putting them on a graph makes the story easy to read.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Find where y = 3x − 1 and y = x + 5 intersect, and check your answer by substitution.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 3x − 1 = x + 5 → 2x = 6 → x = 3, y = 8. The lines meet at (3, 8). Check: x + 5 = 3 + 5 = 8 ✓.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A line passes through (2, 7) and (5, 16). Find its gradient, then its equation in the form y = mx + c.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Gradient = (16 − 7) ÷ (5 − 2) = 9 ÷ 3 = 3. Using (2, 7): 7 = 3(2) + c → c = 1. So the equation is y = 3x + 1. Check: 3(5) + 1 = 16 ✓.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Sagal says, ‘A line with a bigger number in front of x is always steeper.’ Is she right? Explain with an example comparing y = 2x and y = −5x.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: No, Sagal is not quite right. Steepness depends on the size (absolute value) of the gradient, not on whether the number looks ‘bigger’ as a signed value. y = 2x has gradient 2, and y = −5x has gradient −5; since |−5| = 5 is greater than 2, y = −5x is actually the steeper line, even though −5 is less than 2.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: The line y = mx + c passes through (0, 4) and (3, 0). Find m and c.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Since the line passes through (0, 4), c = 4. Gradient m = (0 − 4) ÷ (3 − 0) = −4 ÷ 3 = −4/3. So m = −4/3 and c = 4.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Reading and Interpreting Graphs.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Drawing a graph is only half the skill; the other half is reading one that is already drawn. Graphs answer questions quickly once you know how to look. Direct reading finds a value straight from the line. To answer “what is y when x = 4?”, go up from 4 on the x-axis until you meet the line, then across to the y-axis to read the value. To answer “when is y = 10?”, do the reverse: start at 10 on the y-axis, go across to the line, then down to the x-axis.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Real-Life Graphs.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Graphs describe real situations. On a distance–time graph, time goes on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis: a straight sloping line means steady speed, and a flat horizontal line means the object has stopped. For example, if Hassan cycles at a steady 12 km/h, after t hours he has travelled d = 12t km — a straight line through the origin with gradient 12. Cost graphs often have a fixed charge plus a rate, like a taxi charging 200 shillings plus 100 shillings per kilometre: C = 100d + 200, where 200 is the y-intercept (the starting fee) and 100 is the gradient (the cost per km).

choices: The cost per kilometre
The fixed charge before the taxi moves
The total distance travelled
The speed of the taxi
rounds.answer: The fixed charge before the taxi moves
rounds.clue: This number is the y-intercept — the value of C when d = 0.
rounds.explanation: 150 is the y-intercept: the fixed charge you pay even before travelling, since C = 150 when d = 0.

rounds.prompt: What does “Origin” mean?
choices: The point (0, 0) where the axes cross
One of the four regions of the plane
Steepness: change in y over change in x
Where a line crosses the y-axis (x = 0)
rounds.answer: The point (0, 0) where the axes cross
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 11 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Origin means The point (0, 0) where the axes cross.

rounds.prompt: Which quadrant contains the point (−5, 2)?
choices: Quadrant I
Quadrant II
Quadrant III
Quadrant IV
rounds.answer: Quadrant II
rounds.clue: Check the sign of x first, then the sign of y.
rounds.explanation: x is negative (left) and y is positive (up), so the point lies in Quadrant II (top-left).

rounds.prompt: For y = 2x − 3, what is the y-value when x = 4 (a point you would plot to draw the line)?
rounds.clue: Substitute x = 4 into the equation.
rounds.explanation: y = 2(4) − 3 = 8 − 3 = 5, giving the point (4, 5) to plot.

games.title: Real-Life Round: Coordinates
games.description: Practise coordinates through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: Which ordered pair describes a point 2 units left and 5 units down from the origin?
rounds.clue: Left means negative x; down means negative y.
rounds.explanation: Left means negative x, and down means negative y, so the point is (−2, −5).

rounds.prompt: What does “Quadrant” mean?
choices: One of the four regions of the plane
Steepness: change in y over change in x
Where a line crosses the y-axis (x = 0)
Where a line crosses the x-axis (y = 0)
rounds.answer: One of the four regions of the plane
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 11 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Quadrant means One of the four regions of the plane.

rounds.prompt: For the linear function y = 5x − 3, what is the value of c, the y-intercept?
rounds.clue: In y = mx + c, c is the constant term.
rounds.explanation: In y = mx + c, c is the constant term, so c = −3.

rounds.prompt: A straight-line graph shows y = 10 when x = 2 and y = 20 when x = 4. Using interpolation, what is the best estimate for y when x = 3?
rounds.clue: x = 3 is halfway between x = 2 and x = 4.
rounds.explanation: x = 3 is halfway between 2 and 4, so on a straight line y is halfway between 10 and 20, which is 15.

games.title: Spot the Error: Origin
games.description: Practise origin through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Coordinates” mean?
choices: An ordered pair (x, y) giving a position
The point (0, 0) where the axes cross
One of the four regions of the plane
Steepness: change in y over change in x
rounds.answer: An ordered pair (x, y) giving a position
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 11 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Coordinates means An ordered pair (x, y) giving a position.

rounds.prompt: Point P has coordinates (4, −3). What are the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of P?
rounds.clue: In (x, y), the first number is always the x-coordinate.
rounds.explanation: In (x, y), the first number is the x-coordinate and the second is the y-coordinate, so x = 4 and y = −3.

rounds.prompt: Find the gradient of the line passing through (1, 4) and (3, 10).
rounds.clue: Gradient = change in y ÷ change in x.

rounds.prompt: Find the point where the lines y = x + 1 and y = −x + 5 intersect.
rounds.clue: Set the two expressions for y equal to each other.
rounds.explanation: x + 1 = −x + 5 → 2x = 4 → x = 2; then y = 2 + 1 = 3. The lines meet at (2, 3).

selfAssessment: I can plot and read points in all four quadrants using ordered pairs (x, y).
I can name the axes, the origin, and the four quadrants correctly.
I can understand a linear function and the meaning of y = mx + c.
I can calculate a gradient (slope) as a rate of change and find a y-intercept.
I can draw a straight-line graph using a table of values and using gradient and intercept.
I can read values from a graph, including interpolation and extrapolation.
I can find the point where two lines intersect and explain what it means.
I can interpret real-life graphs such as distance–time and cost graphs.
